Joseph: how was the first week at the hospice?
Anjali: good. tiring. sat with a man called Mr Pinto for two hours today, just holding his hand
Anjali: his daughter couldn't get off work till evening. i said i'd stay
Joseph: that's a lot
Anjali: it felt right. like all those nights in Papa's ward weren't for nothing
Anjali: i know the machines, the beeps, what to say to families in the corridor. i finally know what to DO with all that
Joseph: that makes sense. can i ask something?
Anjali: ok
Joseph: when do you get to just miss him? not help anyone. just miss him
Anjali: ...
Anjali: i haven't really. not since the funeral
Anjali: every time it comes up i sign up for another shift
Joseph: the work is good. you're good at it. but maybe it can't be the only place he goes
Anjali: sunday is his birthday. maybe i'll take it off and go to church with Mummy
Joseph: want company after?
Anjali: yes. thank you

qa.q: How long did Anjali sit with Mr Pinto?
qa.a: Two hours, just holding his hand.

qa.q: Why does the hospice work feel right to Anjali?
qa.a: Anjali feels satisfied that all those nights in Papa's ward weren't for nothing; finally knowing what to do with them turns the loss into purpose.

qa.q: What choice at the end of the chat gives the grief its own space?
qa.a: Taking Sunday, Papa's birthday, off to go to church with Mummy and meeting Joseph afterwards, instead of signing up for another shift.

qa.q: What might Joseph be worried about when asking, "when do you get to just miss him?"
qa.a: Joseph seems worried that Anjali is using the work to avoid grieving, and that the sadness will stay stuck if it only ever turns into helping others.

grounding: Shows an adult who lost a parent to a long illness finding purpose in hospice work, and a friend's question reminding them that the grief itself still needs space.

In the small primary health centre at Sangamner, Vishal, twenty-four, was first to arrive and last to leave. For three years he had taken his mother by local bus to the district hospital for her treatments; since she died in March, he had enrolled as a trainee nursing assistant.
He was good at it. He knew how to lift an old farmer without hurting him, and what to say to a frightened daughter in the corridor. The senior nurse, Usha, watched him calm a whole family in five minutes.
But she also saw him flinch when a patient asked, "Your mother must be proud?" and then hurry off to restock gauze.
That evening Usha stopped him at the gate. "You're very good here, Vishal. But this place can't hold all of it. When did you last sit with your own sadness?"
He didn't answer. On Sunday, for the first time since March, he went to the temple by the river and sat there a long time, not helping anyone.

qa.q: What did Vishal enrol as after his mother died?
qa.a: A trainee nursing assistant at the small primary health centre at Sangamner.

qa.q: Why might restocking gauze feel easier to Vishal than answering the patient's question?
qa.a: The work gives his loss a purpose and keeps him busy, while the question touched the raw grief for his mother that he hadn't let himself feel.

qa.q: What turning point did Usha's question create?
qa.a: It named that the work couldn't hold all of his grief, and on Sunday he sat by the river for a long time, giving the sadness its own space.

qa.q: How does Usha see Vishal's skill with patients?
qa.a: Usha admires how well he calms families, but also notices the flinch and the constant busyness, and cares enough to say what the work can't do.

grounding: Illustrates a young man who turns the loss of his mother after a long illness into nursing work, and a senior nurse who reminds him that grief needs its own space.

Madhuri stopped, put on a posh voice like a TV cook, waved her ruler like a spoon and said, "Today, darlings, we cook the in-GREE-dee-ents!" The whole class cracked up. Even Miss smiled.

Monday. In science, Hafsa, ten, read "photosynthesis" as "photo-sin-thesis". Someone giggled. She held up an invisible camera and said, "Say cheese, everyone, it's photo-sin time!" The class roared, and her ears stopped burning.
Wednesday. It was her turn again. Before she even started, she crossed her eyes and made a fish face. Everyone laughed, waiting for more. "Hafsa, just read, please," said the teacher. That evening she shoved her reading book under the bed. "I'm the funny one, Noor baji," she told her cousin. "Not the reading one."
Saturday. Noor baji sat with her on the floor. They clapped out hard words together: pho-to-syn-the-sis. Hafsa still made jokes, silly ones about plants eating sunshine. But she read the whole next page, stopping only twice.

qa.q: How did Hafsa read "photosynthesis" on Monday?
qa.a: As "photo-sin-thesis".

qa.q: What does "I'm the funny one, not the reading one" reveal about Hafsa's worry?
qa.a: It reveals she worries she is bad at reading, and being funny feels like a safer thing to be known for.

qa.q: What choice by Noor baji on Saturday helped?
qa.a: Practising hard words with Hafsa by clapping out the syllables, without taking her jokes away, so reading felt less scary 🙂

qa.q: What might the teacher be thinking when saying, "Hafsa, just read, please"?
qa.a: The teacher may think Hafsa is just being silly on purpose, without seeing the worry about reading underneath the fish face.

grounding: Illustrates a child who covers reading stumbles with jokes that make the class laugh with her, while the clowning hides a worry that shows at home.

"Di, guess what I said in class today?"
"What?"
"I walked in with the new glasses, and before anyone could say anything I went, 'Good morning, I'm your new headmistress, Mrs Bottle-Bottom.' Everyone died laughing."
"Ha! Brave."
"Right? Nobody could make fun of me, because I got there first."
"So it went fine?"
"...Mostly. At lunch Aryan called me Mrs Bottle-Bottom and the whole table laughed. And in PT. And on the bus."
"Did you laugh?"
"Of course. It's my joke." Sarika pushed the glasses up her nose. "It was just funnier when I said it."
Megha put down her phone. "Sarika, you handed them the joke. Now they think it's allowed."
"So what, I stop being funny?"
"Be funny about other things. You don't have to hit yourself first."

qa.a: Mrs Bottle-Bottom, the new headmistress.

qa.q: Why did Sarika feel safe making the joke first?
qa.a: Getting there first meant nobody could mock her before she did; it gave her control and won laughs instead of teasing 😅

In Class 10 I had a joke for every test. When the maths papers came back, I'd hold mine up before anyone asked: "Nineteen! A personal best. Somebody call the news." People laughed. They liked me for it. It felt much better than waiting for someone to notice.
The trouble came slowly. By December, people started the joke for me. "Ask Payal, she'll know the wrong answer." When I got sixty-eight in the pre-boards, the boys at the back said, "Who did you copy from?" Nobody believed I could just get a good mark.
My best friend Indu was the one who said it. "Payal, you taught them that. You keep telling everyone you're stupid."
I'm in Class 11 now. I still make jokes, just not about my own brain. It's quieter. But when I got a good mark last week, people only said, "Nice."

qa.q: What did Payal say when she held up a nineteen?
qa.a: "Nineteen! A personal best. Somebody call the news."

qa.q: Why did joking first feel better to Payal than waiting?
qa.a: It let her control the moment and win laughs and liking, instead of dreading someone else noticing the low mark.

qa.q: What choice has Payal made since Indu spoke up?
qa.a: She still jokes, just not about her own brain, so classmates no longer treat her as the target and a good mark gets a simple "Nice."

qa.q: Why might the boys at the back ask "Who did you copy from?" after the sixty-eight?
qa.a: They had heard Payal call herself stupid so often that they believed it, so a good mark looked suspicious to them.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who mocked her own marks before anyone else could, winning acceptance until classmates began to see her as the target.

I'm Parveen, and I still think about the afternoon our drone died. Four of us had spent three months building it for the final-year showcase. Test flight, in front of the whole department: it rose beautifully, wobbled, and flew straight into the neem tree by the canteen. It hung there, one propeller turning slowly, as if it were waving at us.
There was a terrible silence. Then Ujjwal said, very seriously, "Well. Technically, it flew." I laughed so hard I had to sit on the steps, and then we were all laughing, though my eyes were stinging for other reasons too.
Afterwards it was easier to breathe. We climbed up, got it down, and sat on the steps with a notebook: two propellers broken, board fine, showcase in nine days. By evening we had a plan and a parts list.
Looking back, the joke didn't make it hurt less. It just made it possible to start.

qa.q: Where did the drone end up?
qa.a: Straight in the neem tree by the canteen.

qa.q: What does "my eyes were stinging for other reasons too" suggest about how Parveen felt?
qa.a: It suggests Parveen was really upset about losing three months of work even while laughing; the humour didn't erase the hurt.

qa.q: Which choice after the laughing got the project moving again?
qa.a: Getting the drone down and listing the damage and the nine days left in a notebook, so the relief from laughing turned straight into a plan 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Ujjwal had snapped, "Whose fault was this?" instead?
qa.a: The silence might have turned into blame, making everyone defensive and slowing the repair, instead of pulling the group together to plan.

grounding: Shows students whose project crashes laughing at the absurdity, which gives distance from the hurt without denying it and lets them start planning.

Lab instructor's note, Monday, R. Fernandes
The cold room failed over the weekend. Mridul and Sumit's six-week crystal samples, the core of their final-year project, had turned into cloudy puddles.
I came in expecting tears or a fight. Instead Sumit held up a flask, studied it and said, "Congratulations. We've invented soup." Mridul started laughing and couldn't stop; he had to put his head down on the bench. I admit I laughed too. Then Mridul's hands started shaking, and he said quietly, "Six weeks, though." Nobody pretended it didn't matter.
After about five minutes they wiped their faces, pulled up the calendar, and asked what could be saved. We agreed on a shorter three-week run, a smaller sample set, and a section in the report on what went wrong.
Next: extension request to the department by Wednesday; get the cold-room alarm checked.

qa.q: What did Sumit say, holding up a flask?
qa.a: "Congratulations. We've invented soup."

qa.q: How can you tell the laughter didn't mean Mridul didn't care?
qa.a: Mridul's hands started shaking and he said quietly, "Six weeks, though", showing real hurt alongside the laughter.

qa.q: Which step came right after the laughing, and why did it matter?
qa.a: They wiped their faces, pulled up the calendar and asked what could be saved, turning relief into a concrete, shorter plan.

qa.q: How might the instructor have felt, walking in expecting tears or a fight?
qa.a: The instructor was probably braced for a hard scene and felt relieved, even laughing too, when the joke eased the room enough to plan.

grounding: Illustrates, in an instructor's note, students laughing at a ruined experiment without denying the loss, then moving straight into planning.

Looking back, I should have noticed sooner. Ira was the funniest person in our group, the one who could turn a delayed train into ten minutes of stand-up. But every time someone asked her something real, she dodged. "How's your dad after the surgery?" "Oh, he's flirting with the nurses, he's fine." "Did you hear back about the job in Pune?" "Pune can't handle me." Then a new joke, a new topic.
At my birthday dinner in October, I watched her keep the table roaring for an hour. Then the bill came, everyone looked at their phones, and her face just switched off. She stared at the candle for a long time.
The next day I texted her, only her: "You were brilliant last night. You also looked tired. Walk on Saturday, no jokes needed?"
Four hours later: "Yes. Please, Aadhya."
Her dad's surgery hadn't gone well.

qa.a: "Oh, he's flirting with the nurses, he's fine."

qa.q: What did Aadhya think when Ira's face "switched off" after the bill came?
qa.a: Aadhya felt concerned, sensing the jokes had been covering something painful and that Ira was worn out once the performing stopped.

qa.q: Why was Aadhya's private text a good choice?
qa.a: It praised Ira, gently named the tiredness and offered a no-pressure walk away from the group, making it safe to stop joking.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ira to read "no jokes needed"?
qa.a: Ira may have felt relieved and seen, as if someone had finally noticed the effort behind the jokes, which is why the answer was "Yes. Please."

Supervisor's note, Trisha, pathology lab, Friday
Deepika has always been our lab's comedian. This month it's constant. When I asked in Monday's review how the move to her new flat was going, she said, "Great, the cockroaches are very welcoming." When Anu asked about her mother's hospital visit, Deepika did an impression of the ward matron and the whole room laughed. Nobody got an answer.
Today, after the team left, I found her still at her bench, not working, just holding a pipette and staring at the window. No jokes. She looked older.
We've been friends since college, so I sat down and said, "I'm not asking as your boss. How are you really? And your mum?" She was quiet, then said, "Not good." We talked for forty minutes.
Next: offer flexible hours next week; check in again on Monday, just the two of us.

qa.q: What did Deepika say about her new flat?
qa.a: "Great, the cockroaches are very welcoming."

qa.q: What did Trisha think on finding Deepika at the bench, staring at the window?
qa.a: Trisha sensed that the joking had stopped and something heavy lay underneath, most likely worry about Deepika's mother.

qa.q: Which choice by Trisha made it safe for Deepika to answer?
qa.a: Waiting until the team had left and saying "I'm not asking as your boss", so the question came from a friend, in private, not in front of the group.

qa.q: What might the team have missed by only laughing at the impressions?
qa.a: They enjoyed the jokes but never noticed that no question got answered, so Deepika's worry about her mother stayed hidden from them.

grounding: Illustrates a friend and supervisor who notices a colleague turning every serious question into a joke and checks in privately once the joking stops.

I'm Jagdish, and I've been sleeping on my sister Preeti's sofa in Nagpur during my exams, so I hear a lot.
Every few evenings Preeti brings up money. Last night she had the electricity bill and the EMI letter in her hand. "Ashwin, we need to decide what we cut back on." Ashwin, honestly the funniest person I know, said, "Easy. We cut back on Jagdish." I laughed. So did he. Preeti smiled a small smile and said, "I mean it."
He did a whole routine about living on air and sunlight. Then he asked what was for dinner.
I don't know exactly what Preeti felt. But she folded the letter into a tiny square and didn't say much after. This morning she was doing sums on the back of an envelope, alone at six, while he slept.
Tonight she asked me to go for a walk so she could talk to Ashwin properly.

qa.q: What did Ashwin say when Preeti asked what they should cut back on?
qa.a: "Easy. We cut back on Jagdish."

qa.a: It suggests she felt dismissed and frustrated, holding the worry alone after the jokes pushed her serious point aside.

qa.q: Which choice by Preeti tonight could change the pattern?
qa.a: Asking for time alone with Ashwin; she can tell him plainly that the jokes make her feel unheard and that the bills need one serious talk.

qa.a: Jagdish may feel a little uneasy, seeing that the laugh helped push Preeti's serious point aside, which may be why Jagdish watched her so closely afterwards.

passage:
Last March, if you'd asked me, I'd have said Neelam was the most perfect friend in the world. She shared her headphones on every bus ride, did my hair for annual day, and knew what I was thinking before I did. I wrote her name inside my compass box.
Then on my fifteenth birthday she didn't message me until nine at night. Nine. I checked my phone all day. By evening, in my head, she had become a fake, a traitor, someone who had probably never liked me. I told two girls she was "two-faced" and scratched her name out of the compass box.
Her message, when it came, said: "Sorry Gargi, Nani was in hospital all day."
I'm sixteen now. I still feel that switch sometimes, all good to all bad in one second. I'm learning to wait before I scratch anything out.

qa.q: When did Neelam message Gargi on the birthday?
qa.a: Not until nine at night.

qa.q: Why did Neelam go from perfect to "a traitor" so fast in Gargi's mind?
qa.a: The hurt of waiting all day was so strong that Gargi couldn't hold Neelam's good sides and this one disappointment together, so the whole picture flipped.

qa.q: What is Gargi learning to do when the switch comes?
qa.a: To wait before scratching anything out, giving time to find out what really happened before deciding a friend is all bad.

qa.q: What might Neelam feel on hearing she'd been called "two-faced"?
qa.a: Neelam, who had spent the day at the hospital with Nani, would likely feel hurt and confused at being judged so harshly for a late message.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees a friend as perfect and then as a traitor after one late birthday message, unable in that moment to hold both sides together.

School counsellor's note, Noor, Class 9
Thomas came in on Tuesday, sent by his class teacher after an argument in the corridor. Two weeks ago, in this same room, he described Akshay as "basically the perfect friend, never lets anyone down". Today Akshay was "a snake", "fake from the start", "the worst person in the school". The reason: Akshay had picked someone else as his partner for the science fair.
Thomas talked fast, fists tight. I didn't argue. I asked him to tell me three things Akshay had done this year. He listed them: stood up for him when seniors took his bat, shared notes when he had jaundice, and chose a different partner. He went quiet. "Two good, one bad," he said. "I guess he's not a snake."
Next: meet Thursday; suggest Thomas tell Akshay directly that he felt left out.

qa.q: Why was Akshay "the worst person in the school" to Thomas that day?
qa.a: Akshay had picked someone else as his partner for the science fair.

qa.q: Why did one slight wipe out everything good for Thomas?
qa.a: Feeling left out hurt so much that he couldn't hold Akshay's kindness and this disappointment at the same time, so Akshay flipped from perfect to a snake.

qa.q: What did Noor's "three things" question do well?
qa.a: It helped Thomas lay the good and the disappointing side by side himself, so he could see Akshay as a whole person again.

qa.q: How might Akshay feel if Thomas says he felt left out, instead of calling him a snake?
qa.a: Akshay would probably understand and feel less attacked, and could explain the choice or include Thomas next time.

"Pallavi, last month your guide was a legend and today she's useless? Sit with your Himani bua a minute.
At nineteen, in Delhi, I worshipped Professor Rajan. I copied his handwriting. I told everyone he was the only real historian in the country. I sat in the front row with my notebook open like a prayer book.
Then he handed back my term paper with one line: 'Lazy argument. You can do far better.' That was all. By evening he was, according to me, a snob, an old fraud who hadn't written anything new in years. I skipped his classes for a month and told my roommate he was finished.
Years later I read that paper again. He was right. It was lazy. He wasn't a god, and he wasn't a fraud. He was a good teacher who said one thing too bluntly.
I put him so high, beta, that one ordinary flaw felt like a fall."

qa.a: Rereading the paper years later and admitting it was lazy, which let her see a good teacher who was too blunt, not a god or a fraud.

The fellowship portal closed at midnight, the hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping, and Mahima still needed Dr Sharmila's letter uploaded. At eight, Dr Sharmila emailed back her statement of purpose with one comment: "This reads like a school essay. Cut the first page."
Mahima read it on the corridor floor, next to the only socket that worked. For two semesters Dr Sharmila had been "the only real scientist in the department". Mahima had copied her way of labelling samples and quoted her at dinner.
Now, typing to her roommate, she wrote: "She's so bitter. Honestly, she's overrated. Her last paper was nothing." Each line felt good for a second.
At ten, with the Wi-Fi back, Mahima opened the draft. The first page was, in fact, mostly throat-clearing. She stared at it, jaw tight, torn between cutting it and never asking that woman for anything again.

passage:
In Hoshangabad, Kamini, nineteen, spent the Diwali rush behind the counter of her father's sweet shop, weighing kaju katli until her arms ached. Her phone buzzed twice in her apron pocket. She couldn't answer; the queue went out the door.
For months Rajni, from her teacher-training college, had called Kamini "the only one in this whole town who understands me". The next morning at the bus stand, Rajni wouldn't look at her. "She's useless," Rajni told the other girls loudly. "Selfish. When I actually need someone, gone."
Kamini's face burned. She wanted to shout back that Rajni was being dramatic. She didn't. She walked over and said quietly, "I missed your call because I was at the shop. I'm sorry. I can't answer during shop hours, but I'm free after eight tonight if you want to talk."
Rajni turned away. Kamini got on the bus, hands still shaking, and didn't take back a word.

qa.q: Why couldn't Kamini answer Rajni's calls?

qa.q: How did Kamini feel at the bus stand, and what shows it?

qa.q: Which choice by Kamini kept a steady boundary without reacting in kind?

qa.q: Why might Rajni flip from "the only one who understands me" to "useless"?

I didn't take sides. Each time he brought me a hero or a villain, I asked the same thing: 'What exactly happened? What was said, and when?' Usually the answer was one small event. I wrote down the facts, dealt with those, and treated everyone the same in meetings.

qa.q: Who was "the only person who actually works here" in June?

qa.q: Why might Vimal's labels have felt true to him each time?

qa.q: What question did Bhavna ask, and why did it help?

qa.q: How might the housekeeping head have felt going from praised to "a snake"?
qa.a: She would likely feel confused and wary, since one question about a booking suddenly turned praise into hostility.

grounding: Shows, through a senior manager's memory, a manager who notices a staff member sorting colleagues into saints and enemies and responds by asking for specifics and staying fair.

It was the week before Diwali, the warehouse in Guwahati was running double shifts, and half the loading team was out with flu. Siddharth, twenty-five and three months into his first manager job, had forty trucks to dispatch by Friday.
Pradeep caught him by the loading bay. "Sir, Moni is useless. She's sabotaging my shift. Everyone knows it." Last month Moni had been "the only one here I trust". And yesterday's villain, Ravi from inventory, was apparently a hero today.
Siddharth had no time for this. It would have been easy to nod and move Moni off the shift. Instead he opened the notes on his phone. "Okay. What exactly happened, and when?"
Pradeep paused. "Yesterday. The truck left twenty minutes late."
"Because?"
"...The pallets weren't wrapped. That was my part, actually. She was waiting on me."
Siddharth wrote it down, kept Moni on the shift, and asked both of them to meet him after the rush.

qa.q: How late did the truck leave?
qa.a: Twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have been thinking when it would have been easy to nod along?
qa.a: Siddharth was probably stressed and tempted to take Pradeep's word with forty trucks and staff out sick, but he seemed to sense that fairness needed the facts first.

qa.q: What did asking for specifics reveal, and why did it matter?
qa.a: It showed the delay came from Pradeep's own unwrapped pallets, not Moni, so Siddharth could keep Moni on the shift and stay fair to everyone.

qa.q: What would change for Moni if Siddharth had simply moved her off the shift?
qa.a: Moni would have been punished for someone else's delay and branded a villain, likely feeling bewildered and losing trust in her manager.

grounding: Illustrates a new manager under festival-rush pressure who notices a team member casting colleagues as heroes and villains and asks for the specific facts before acting.
